walkthroughs.body_html:
Resources & Their Management — a core area of GCSE Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Resources & Their Management brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Resources & Their Management.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Who argued food can't keep up with population (1798)?
options: Darwin
Malthus
Marx
Smith

mcqs.q: Shift from high to low birth/death rates is called?
options: Demographic transition
Carrying capacity
Population pyramid
Mortality crisis

mcqs.q: Roughly what proportion of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
options: About 50 percent.
About 10 percent.
100 percent (everything transfers).

mcqs.q: Why is a cold winter not evidence against climate change?

It is evidence - if it gets cold sometimes, warming must be wrong.

Cold winters are caused by warming.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Demographic transition”?
options: Bar chart by age and sex; shape reveals demographic stage and future trends.
Shift from high birth and death rates to low rates as societies industrialise.
Area of productive land needed to sustain a person's consumption and absorb their waste.
Thomas Malthus (1798) argued population grows faster than food supply, causing crises.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Population pyramid”?
options: Faster use of non-renewables (minerals, fossil fuels) than they form or can be substituted.
Shift from high birth and death rates to low rates as societies industrialise.
Thomas Malthus (1798) argued population grows faster than food supply, causing crises.
Bar chart by age and sex; shape reveals demographic stage and future trends.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Resource depletion”?
options: Faster use of non-renewables (minerals, fossil fuels) than they form or can be substituted.
Area of productive land needed to sustain a person's consumption and absorb their waste.
Shift from high birth and death rates to low rates as societies industrialise.
Maximum population an environment can sustainably support.
